title: Find a conditional probability from a table or counts
applies: The question asks for a probability given that another event occurred. Counts are usable for equally likely observations.
steps: Identify B, the given event, and use it as the restricted sample space.
Count or compute the intersection A∩B.
Divide the intersection count or probability by the corresponding count or probability for B.
pitfalls: P(A|B) and P(B|A) generally use different denominators.
A zero-probability condition needs a different setup.
checks: The answer is between zero and one. The numerator cannot exceed the denominator.

example.problem: Of 12 students, 7 take music, 5 play a sport, and 3 do both. Given sport, find the probability of music.
example.answer: Restrict to the 5 sport students. Of those, 3 take music, so the probability is 3/5.

title: Compute the expected value of a discrete distribution
pattern: E[X]=Σ x P(X=x) when the expectation exists
applies: The outcomes and their probabilities are available, and the weighted sum is well defined.
steps: List the values of the variable and their probabilities.
Multiply each value by its probability and sum the products.
Use net gains after any fees when asked about profit.
pitfalls: An expected value can differ from every possible outcome.
A fair game has expected net gain zero, even if the wins and losses are unequal.
checks: Probabilities sum to one. For a finite distribution the mean lies between its smallest and largest possible values.

example.problem: A game pays a net gain of −2 with probability 3/4 and +6 with probability 1/4. Find the expected gain.
example.answer: (−2)(3/4)+6(1/4)=0, so it is fair in expectation.

title: Compute probabilities for a binomial count
applies: There are a fixed number of independent two-outcome trials with the same success probability.
steps: Define a success and identify n and p.
For exactly k, multiply the number of success positions by the probability of any one arrangement.
For at least or at most, sum the appropriate terms or use the shorter complementary event.
pitfalls: At least k includes k.
Sampling without replacement from a finite population generally changes the success probability.
checks: Check that k is an integer in [0,n]. All n+1 binomial probabilities sum to one.

example.problem: Find the chance of exactly 2 successes in 5 independent trials with p=1/4.

title: Convert a normal probability to a standard normal z-score
pattern: z=(x−μ)/σ and P(X≤x)=Φ(z) for X∼N(μ,σ²), σ>0
applies: The random variable is normal, or a justified normal approximation is part of the problem.
steps: Identify the mean and standard deviation. Take the square root if given the variance.
Standardize each boundary with the same mean and standard deviation.
Use the standard normal CDF, complement, or difference of CDF values for the requested region.
pitfalls: A right-tail probability uses 1−Φ(z). A sample mean generally uses its standard error.
checks: Sketch the shaded region, verify the direction of each tail, and check that Φ(0)=1/2.

example.problem: X is normal with mean 50 and standard deviation 4. Approximate P(X≤54).

title: Test one population mean using a known standard deviation
applies: The population standard deviation is known and observations are independent. The sample mean has a justified normal distribution or approximation.
steps: State the null mean and directional or two-sided alternative before looking at the result.
Compute the standard error and the z statistic under the null.
Read the p-value in the tail or tails specified by the alternative. Compare with the chosen significance level and state the conclusion in context.
pitfalls: An unknown σ usually calls for a t procedure under its assumptions.
The p-value is a probability of data at least as extreme under the null, rather than the probability the null is true.
checks: The test statistic is unitless and the p-value is in [0,1]. Check the alternative matches the number and direction of tails.

example.problem: For n=25, x̄=102, σ=5, and H₀: μ=100, find the two-sided p-value.

title: Choose permutations or combinations for counting selections
applies: You choose k objects without replacement from n distinguishable objects.
steps: Decide whether changing the order makes a different outcome.
For ordered choices, multiply the number of available choices for successive positions.
For unordered choices, divide by k! because each k-element subset has k! orders.
pitfalls: Replacement or repeated indistinguishable objects changes the counting model.
checks: For unordered choices, C(n,k)=C(n,n−k). The ordered count must equal k! times the unordered count.

example.problem: From 8 people choose a 3-person committee, then separately count ways to assign three distinct roles.
example.answer: There are C(8,3)=56 committees and 8·7·6=336 assignments.

title: Compute the sample mean, variance, and standard deviation
applies: A list of quantitative observations is given and the task distinguishes a sample from a complete population.
steps: Compute the arithmetic mean.
Subtract the mean from each observation, square the differences, and sum them.
Divide by n−1 for sample variance or by n for population variance. Take the square root for standard deviation.
pitfalls: Variance has squared units; standard deviation has the original units.
Keep intermediate values exact to avoid rounding the mean too early.
checks: The deviations sum to zero before rounding. Both variance and standard deviation are nonnegative.

example.problem: Find the mean and sample variance of 2, 4, 6, 8.
example.answer: The mean is 5 and the squared deviations sum to 20, so s²=20/3.

title: Compute compound interest with matching time and rate units
pattern: A=P(1+r/n)^(nt) for nominal annual rate r and n compounding periods per year
applies: The rate and compounding convention are specified and no additional cash flows are present.
steps: Convert the annual percentage rate to a decimal and identify periods per year.
Use the per-period rate r/n and total number of periods nt.
Solve for future value, present value, or time as requested, using a logarithm for an unknown exponent when valid.
pitfalls: An effective annual rate already includes compounding for a year.
Round currency at the end unless the problem states a period-by-period rounding rule.
checks: At t=0 the result is P. With positive rate and time the amount exceeds the starting principal.

example.problem: Find the value of 800 after 2 years at 5% compounded annually.

title: Differentiate sums and powers term by term
pattern: d(c x^p)/dx=c p x^(p−1) where the power is differentiable
applies: The expression is a finite sum of constants and constant multiples of powers of the variable.
steps: Rewrite simple reciprocal terms as negative powers and constants as degree zero.
Bring down each nonzero exponent as a factor and subtract one from it.
Sum the derivatives and preserve the original function's relevant domain restrictions.
pitfalls: A constant contributes zero.
A power of a nontrivial inner expression requires the chain rule.
checks: Check term degrees and signs, and verify a point numerically only within the domain.

title: Differentiate an accumulation integral with variable limits
applies: The integrand depends on its integration variable only, is continuous on the relevant interval, and the bounds are differentiable.
steps: Identify the upper and lower limits as functions of x.
Evaluate the integrand at each limit and multiply by the derivative of that limit.
Subtract the lower-limit contribution from the upper-limit contribution.
pitfalls: A variable bound contributes its derivative factor.
If the integrand also depends explicitly on x, differentiation under the integral needs an additional term and suitable hypotheses.
checks: A constant bound contributes zero and identical bounds give derivative zero.

example.problem: Differentiate the integral of cos(t) from 2 to x².
example.answer: The upper contribution is cos(x²)·2x and the lower contribution is zero.

title: Compute the area between curves by integrating their difference
applies: Two graphs bound a region on a known interval, or its endpoints can be found from intersections.
steps: Find the endpoints and solve for any interior intersections.
On each subinterval, determine the upper graph and subtract the lower graph.
Integrate the difference on each interval and add the nonnegative areas. Use right minus left for horizontal slices.
pitfalls: Net signed integral can cancel positive geometric area.
Split anywhere the order of the curves changes.
checks: Area is nonnegative and has squared units. A sketch or a test point can verify curve order.

example.problem: Find the area between y=x and y=x² on [0,1].
example.answer: x≥x² on this interval, so the area is ∫₀¹(x−x²)dx=1/6.
